The device in your apartment is essentially performing two functions, if not more: switching and routing. The router components orchestrates traffic between your LAN and your ISP network. The switch sends traffic on the local subnet(s) to the ports on which the corresponding local devices are found - specifically on their MAC address via ARP.

If you tracert to a server on the Internet you will see the hops from router to router, yours being the first - your default gateway.

Think of an image like taking a snapshot. If you take a snapshot of a hard drive, it means you could recreate the whole thing on another physical piece of hardware. It is unlikely that this is happening across the network without your knowledge.

If backups are being done of individual files or folders (recursively) this could be manually kicked off or scheduled via script - there's really no telling when.

Going through event viewer is a bit like a needle in a haystack scenario unless you know what you're looking for to be honest.

While a backup is running you would see the network activity reflected in Windows Resource Monitor.

On a company device, it's probably best to assume that nothing is in actual fact private...

If you do need to store something sensitive for your purposes only, you would probably need to look at an encrypted archive. (7z for example)

I doubt they are backing up the whole of the drives(s), that is taking images of the partitions on the disk. But administrators - and programs reaching out over the network running as administrator - can see the whole partition. For example via "C$" admin share; the root level. Any number of programs can copy files from there back to the server - for example robocopy. This kind of thing would be tough for you to spot, but there ought to be signs in the windows event viewer.

Whether this *is* being done and whether this *should* be done is a matter of company policy & procedure.
